newsitem.title: INDIA: Investors warned to steer clear of Indian stocks.
newsitem.headline: Investors warned to steer clear of Indian stocks.

text.p: Indian stocks may have been soaring recently, but investors would do well to avoid the country's volatile share markets until prices stabilise, analysts said on Thursday.
Before Thursday, the key 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index had jumped 40 percent in six weeks since hitting three-year lows on December 4.

But the index contracted by a hefty five percent on Thursday after an initial surge, and analysts said more such volatility could be expected as the recent market rally was not supported by fundamentals. They said those who invested too heavily in the markets were flirting with disaster.
"Investors should keep away," said Sanjeev Choithani, chief dealer at broker Pashupati Advani. "Get out and stay out."

The prolonged rally was sparked by government promises of tax breaks and other incentives aimed at reviving sagging industrial growth and jump-starting the markets, and expectations of a pick-up in foreign fund-buying.

The cash-starved government wants vibrant capital markets, seeing them as essential to the success of its programme to divest itself of state assets. The programme is budgeted to raise 50 billion rupees during 1996/97 (April-March).

Aspi Contractor, research head at securities firm Ceat Financial, said market players were building up long positions in stocks in hopes they could sell them at higher prices later when anticipated demand picks up.
Some market players are reportedly using borrowed funds to compile their long positions.
Foreign funds have not been aggressive buyers, but the huge gains have begun to lure unwary investors into the fray, market watchers warned.

Analysts warned that most companies could expect to report a profit squeeze for the year to March 31, 1997, with some showing negative growth due to increased competition, higher costs and slowing demand.
"Investors should wait till a clearer picture emerges," said Antony Sequeira, a director at Arcadia Share and Stock Brokers.
Other analysts were more forceful. "We recommend a total suspension of buying and a phased disinvestment programme," ING Barings analyst Praween Napate said.
In a daily note on Thursday headlined, "Red alert: Market has entered the danger zone," he said he did not see fundamentals improving in the near future.
The benchmark top-30 index of the Bombay Stock Exchange on Thursday fell 193.12 points, or 5.30 percent, to a provisional 3,453.61 at close -- after zooming to 3,812.31 in the morning.
The 50-share National Stock Exchange followed the BSE downward, losing 33.00 points, or 3.17 percent, to end at 1,009.
"The extreme volatility is very unique in Indian markets," said Ceat's Contractor. "It looks apprehensive."
Analysts said domestic funds, some of them facing redemptions, sold heavily to cool the market. Local players also booked profits ahead of the close of weekly settlement on Friday at the BSE.
